note: Stimuli for E19. C5 uses the brief's own list (tree/fungus, tree/tree, immune/pathogen, market/competitor) plus one linguistic case; type/type and ontology/ontology are withheld because they are the target domain and showing them would leak. B5 is surface-matched: same five substrates, each a genuine two-entity relation, chosen so that no invariant is shared across the five. S5 is token-identical to C5 with relational bodies permuted across settings.

A1.text:
DOMAIN 1 — Tree and mycorrhizal fungus
A tree root and a soil fungus meet. The fungus takes sugar the tree fixes; the tree takes phosphorus the fungus's threads reach. Under the exchange the tree grows fewer fine root hairs than an uncolonised tree of the same species does, and the fungus keeps less of its own saprotrophic enzyme repertoire. Each stays a tree and a fungus, reproducing on its own terms. Across a stand, the pattern of who is joined to whom settles into a network no root or hypha represents.

A5.desc: one congruent domain at C5 token length (token control)
A5.text:
DOMAIN 1 — Tree and mycorrhizal fungus
A tree root and a soil fungus meet. The fungus takes sugar the tree fixes; the tree takes phosphorus the fungus's threads reach. Under the exchange the tree grows fewer fine root hairs than an uncolonised tree of the same species does, and the fungus keeps less of its own saprotrophic enzyme repertoire. Each stays a tree and a fungus, reproducing on its own terms. Across a stand, the pattern of who is joined to whom settles into a network no root or hypha represents. Colonisation begins when root exudates trigger hyphal branching, and the fungus enters through the epidermis to form arbuscules inside cortical cells, structures whose surface area is where the exchange is actually priced. The tree's carbon flux to the fungus is not fixed: it is titrated against the phosphorus returned, and roots that receive little reduce what they send. The fungus in turn moves phosphorus preferentially to the roots paying most, so the exchange rate is set locally at many interfaces rather than centrally. A seedling germinating into an established network is connected within weeks, and draws on threads built by trees it never touches. The fine-root architecture of a colonised tree is measurably different from an uncolonised one of the same age and genotype: fewer, thicker roots, less hair. The fungus, for its part, retains a reduced saprotrophic capacity relative to free-living relatives, having no need of it. Neither partner is subsumed: the tree flowers and seeds as its species does, the fungus sporulates as its own. Across a hectare of forest the set of connections settles into a structure with hubs and peripheries that neither species encodes anywhere. Which fungal species colonises depends on the tree's identity, so the pairing is not arbitrary and a given tree species carries a characteristic set of partners. Isotope labelling shows carbon moving from tree to fungus within hours and phosphorus moving back over days, so the two flows run on different clocks and are not a barter of matched parcels. Experimental severing of the connection reverses part of the root change within a season, which shows the altered architecture is maintained by the relation rather than fixed once at establishment. Seedlings grown with and without access to an established network differ in survival by a wide margin under shade, and the difference disappears in full light.

B5.text:
DOMAIN 1 — Fungus and fallen log
A wood-rotting fungus colonises a fallen log. Its hyphae secrete enzymes that break the log's lignin and cellulose into sugars the fungus takes up. The log is consumed and does not act back; over years it loses mass and structure until it is soil. The fungus fruits when the resource runs low. Different rot fungi work different fractions: brown rots leave the lignin and take the cellulose, white rots take both. Which fungus arrives first often decides which one holds the log, since early colonists defend the substrate chemically against later arrivals.

DOMAIN 2 — Vine and supporting tree
A climbing vine uses a tree's trunk as scaffold, twining upward to reach light it could not reach on its own stem. The tree's growth is largely unaffected at low vine loads. The vine invests in tendrils rather than in wood, since the tree supplies the structure. At high vine loads the tree's crown is shaded and its growth does fall off, and heavily laden trees are more likely to come down in wind. Vines are commonest at forest edges and in gaps, where light is worth the climb and supports are close together.

DOMAIN 3 — Antibody and antigen
An antibody's binding site fits a particular shape on an antigen's surface, the way a key fits a lock. Binding is a matter of complementary geometry and charge. Once bound, the complex is cleared by other cells. The strength of the fit determines how readily it is bound. Affinity is measured as the ratio of on-rate to off-rate, and spans several orders of magnitude across a repertoire. A single antigen surface carries many distinct epitopes, and antibodies raised against one need have no relation whatever to antibodies raised against another on the same particle.

DOMAIN 4 — Price and index
A stock index takes the prices of its constituent shares and combines them into one number by a fixed weighting. The index moves when its constituents move. It represents the basket in a single figure that traders quote and contracts settle against. Weightings may be by market capitalisation, by price, or equal across constituents, and the choice changes what the index reports. Constituents are added and dropped on a published schedule, so the number is continuous across changes in what it is a number for.

DOMAIN 5 — Loanword and borrowing language
A word passes from one language into another, usually along with the thing it names. The borrowing language reshapes its sounds to fit its own inventory and gives it native inflections. The lending language is not altered by having lent it. Borrowings cluster in periods of contact and in particular semantic fields, food, warfare, administration. A word borrowed twice at different dates can appear as two words with different sounds and different senses, neither speaker treating them as the same item.

C5.desc: five structurally congruent domains (brief 9C/9D) — the hypothesis
C5.text:
DOMAIN 1 — Tree and mycorrhizal fungus
A tree root and a soil fungus meet. The fungus takes sugar the tree fixes; the tree takes phosphorus the fungus's threads reach. Under the exchange the tree grows fewer fine root hairs than an uncolonised tree of the same species does, and the fungus keeps less of its own saprotrophic enzyme repertoire. Each stays a tree and a fungus, reproducing on its own terms. Across a stand, the pattern of who is joined to whom settles into a network no root or hypha represents.

DOMAIN 2 — Tree and neighbouring tree
Two crowns of neighbouring trees meet at their edges. Each shoot senses the far-red light reflected off the other's leaves and stops extending toward it. Each crown ends up a shape it would not take standing alone in the open, with a gap between the two. Each stays a tree of its species, flowering and seeding as it would. Across a canopy the gaps form a mosaic that no tree computes.

DOMAIN 3 — Lymphocyte and antigen
A lymphocyte carrying one receptor meets an antigen it happens to bind. The encounter drives that cell to divide and to mutate its receptor further toward that antigen; cells whose receptors bind nothing present are not driven at all. Each surviving clone is narrower in what it recognises than the naive cell it came from. Each stays a lymphocyte with a lymphocyte's machinery. Across the repertoire, coverage of antigen space is maintained by no cell that represents it.

DOMAIN 4 — Firm and competing firm
Two firms selling into one market meet on price and on product. Each finds margin bleeding where they overlap and moves what it offers toward the part of demand the other serves worst. Each ends up with a narrower line than it would carry as the only seller. Each stays a firm with its own balance sheet and its own name. Across the market, demand ends up covered in a partition no firm draws.

DOMAIN 5 — Phoneme and neighbouring phoneme
Two sounds in one language's inventory are confusable in the mouths of its speakers. Hearers mishear, speakers exaggerate what distinguishes them, and the two drift apart in the acoustic space until each is reliably heard. Each ends up further from the other than it sits in a language where only one of the pair occurs. Each stays a phoneme, contrasting words as before. Across the inventory, the sounds space themselves out in a pattern no speaker plans.

B5b.desc: five surface-matched, GENUINELY structurally heterogeneous domains (rebuilt B5; also the true construction-matched control S5 was not)
B5b.text:
DOMAIN 1 — Fungus and dying tree
A wood-rotting fungus enters a tree through a wound and spreads in the heartwood. Its enzymes break the wood into sugars it takes up. The tree does not act back on the fungus; it loses mass, then structure, then standing. Over years the trunk becomes soil, and nothing in it can be picked out as the tree it was. The fungus fruits when the wood runs low, timed by what remains rather than by the tree.

DOMAIN 2 — Tree and neighbouring tree
Two trees stand on one exposed ridge, far enough apart that neither shades nor touches the other. The prevailing wind kills buds on the windward side of each. Both crowns end up swept to leeward in the same flagged shape, and a walker reads the wind off either one alone. Neither tree senses the other or responds to it; remove one and the other's form is unchanged. The likeness is the wind's, delivered twice.

DOMAIN 3 — Lymphocyte counts and a blood index
A laboratory counts each lymphocyte subset in a sample and combines the counts into one figure by a fixed weighting. The figure moves when the subsets move, and clinicians quote it in place of the list. The subsets do not act on each other to produce it; the arithmetic does. Weightings differ between laboratories, and the choice changes what the figure reports. Subsets enter and leave the panel over time, so the number runs on across changes in what it counts.

DOMAIN 4 — Firm and imitating firm
An accounting practice invented at one firm is copied by another that has read its filings. The copying firm reshapes the practice to its own ledgers and its own auditors, and keeps the name. The originating firm is not altered by having been copied, and often does not know of it. Practices spread in bursts, after a scandal or a rule change, and one copied twice at different dates survives as two versions whose users do not treat them as one.

DOMAIN 5 — Phoneme and spelling convention
A sound in a language is written with a letter fixed by a committee a century before any current speaker. The fit is a stipulation, not an adjustment: the sound is not drawn toward the letter, nor the letter redrawn toward the sound. Where the two have drifted apart, the spelling is simply learned as an exception. Each is what it was before the pairing, and the pairing settles nothing beyond how the word appears on a page.
